name: Thucydides on how civil war changes the meaning of words
text: Words had to change their ordinary meaning and to take that which was now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation was held to be a cloak for unmanliness; ability to see all sides of a question, inaptness to act on any. Frantic violence became the attribute of manliness; cautious plotting, a justifiable means of self-defence. The advocate of extreme measures was always trustworthy; his opponent a man to be suspected.
author: Thucydides
work: History of the Peloponnesian War, III.82
witness: An Athenian general turned exile writing about the civil war on Corcyra in 427 BCE as a pattern for all such wars. He generalises from one island and writes as a moralist; Crawley's Victorian English (1874) smooths a famously knotted Greek passage.

name: Hobbes on life without a common power
text: In such condition, there is no place for Industry; because the fruit thereof is uncertain; and consequently no Culture of the Earth; no Navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by Sea; no commodious Building; no Instruments of moving, and removing such things as require much force; no Knowledge of the face of the Earth; no account of Time; no Arts; no Letters; no Society; and which is worst of all, continuall feare, and danger of violent death; And the life of man, solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.
author: Thomas Hobbes
witness: Written in Parisian exile at the end of the English civil wars by a royalist who wanted any strong sovereign. The "state of nature" is a thought experiment, not ethnography, though Hobbes points to America and to civil war as examples.

name: Polybius on the cycle of constitutions
text: This is the regular cycle of constitutional revolutions, and the natural order in which constitutions change, are transformed, and return again to their original stage. If a man have a clear grasp of these principles he may perhaps make a mistake as to the dates at which this or that will happen to a particular constitution; but he will rarely be entirely mistaken as to the stage of growth or decay at which it has arrived, or as to the point at which it will undergo some revolutionary change.
author: Polybius
witness: A Greek hostage in Rome, close to the Scipios, explaining to Greeks why Rome had beaten them. The anacyclosis is borrowed from Plato and tidied into a law; it served his argument that Rome's mixed constitution could delay the cycle.

name: Gibbon on the immoderate greatness of Rome
text: But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the causes of destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest; and as soon as time or accident had removed the artificial supports, the stupendous fabric yielded to the pressure of its own weight. The story of its ruin is simple and obvious; and instead of inquiring why the Roman empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it had subsisted so long.
author: Edward Gibbon
work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 38, General Observations
witness: An Enlightenment Englishman summing up the fall of the West for readers who saw Britain's empire in Rome's. Gibbon blamed Christianity and barbarism elsewhere; this passage is an early statement of overreach as a cause, close to Tainter.

name: Procopius on the dim sun of 536
text: And it came about during this year that a most dread portent took place. For the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse, for the beams it shed were not clear nor such as it is accustomed to shed. And from the time when this thing happened men were free neither from war nor pestilence nor any other thing leading to death.
author: Procopius
witness: Belisarius's secretary, writing in Constantinople in the 550s about the year he spent in Sicily and Africa. The dimmed sun is confirmed by tree rings and ice-core sulphate from eruptions in 536 and 540; his link to later war and plague is hindsight.

name: Malthus on the two unequal powers
text: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio. A slight acquaintance with numbers will shew the immensity of the first power in comparison of the second.
author: T. R. Malthus
work: An Essay on the Principle of Population, ch. 1
witness: An English clergyman answering Godwin and Condorcet's hopes of perfectibility, on the eve of the industrial growth that broke his trap. The ratios are rhetoric, not measurement, but the idea of checks underlies every neo-Malthusian and structural-demographic model.

name: Machiavelli on the circle of governments
text: suddenly, liberty passed into license, wherein neither private worth nor public authority was respected, but, every one living as he liked, a thousand wrongs were done daily. Whereupon, whether driven by necessity, or on the suggestion of some wiser man among them and to escape anarchy, the people reverted to a monarchy, from which, step by step, in the manner and for the causes already assigned, they came round once more to license. For this is the circle revolving within which all States are and have been governed; although in the same State the same forms of Government rarely repeat themselves, because hardly any State can have such vitality as to pass through such a cycle more than once
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
work: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, I.2
witness: A Florentine official out of office after the Medici return, retelling Polybius for readers of Livy. He adds that few states live long enough to go round the circle twice: they are conquered first.

name: The opening of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms
text: Empires wax and wane; states cleave asunder and coalesce. When the rule of Chou weakened seven contending principalities sprang up, warring one with another till they settled down as Tsʻin and when its destiny had been fulfilled arose Chʻu and Han to contend for the mastery. And Han was the victor.
author: Luo Guanzhong
work: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, ch. 1
witness: The fourteenth-century novel opens with the Chinese dynastic cycle as a law of history, before telling the fall of the Han after the Yellow Turbans. Fiction, written a millennium after the events, but it shaped how Chinese readers saw order and chaos.

name: Volney among the ruins of Palmyra
text: Here, said I, once flourished an opulent city; here was the seat of a powerful empire. Yes! these places now so wild and desolate, were once animated by a living multitude; a busy crowd thronged in these streets, now so solitary. Within these walls, where now reigns the silence of death, the noise of the arts, and the shouts of joy and festivity incessantly resounded; these piles of marble were regular palaces; these fallen columns adorned the majesty of temples;
author: C.-F. Volney
work: The Ruins, or Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires, ch. 2
witness: A French traveller of the 1780s turned revolutionary deputy, using the ruins of Palmyra to argue that empires fall through despotism and superstition. Read as political allegory, not archaeology.

name: Ammianus on the arrival of the Huns
text: The following circumstances were the original cause of all the destruction and various calamities which the fury of Mars roused up, throwing everything into confusion by his usual ruinous violence: the people called Huns, slightly mentioned in the ancient records, live beyond the Sea of Azov, on the border of the Frozen Ocean, and are a race savage beyond all parallel.
author: Ammianus Marcellinus
witness: A Greek-speaking former Roman officer writing in Rome about fifteen years after Adrianople. He never saw a Hun; his ethnography recycles classical stereotypes of Scythians, but his causal claim, that the Huns started the chain, is the basis of Heather's account.

name: Hesiod on the race of iron
text: For now truly is a race of iron, and men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, and from perishing by night
author: Hesiod
witness: A Boeotian farmer-poet around 700 BCE, after the Dark Age, imagining a decline from golden to iron races. The myth may remember a lost Bronze Age world; it is moral poetry, not history.

name: Ibn Khaldun: religion doubles group feeling
text: La religion, avons-nous dit, est une teinture au moyen de laquelle on fait disparaître les sentiments de jalousie et d'envie qui régnent chez les peuples animés d'un fort esprit de corps. Elle donne à tous les cœurs la même direction, celle de la vérité. ... il agit avec un ensemble parfait, visant toujours au même but et s'exposant à la mort pour parvenir à ses fins.
author: Ibn Khaldun
work: Muqaddimah, ch. 3 (Les Prolégomènes, tr. de Slane, I, p. 284-285)
witness: A Tunisian scholar-official, veteran of Maghrebi court politics, writing in 1377 in retreat at Qal'at Ibn Salama. His examples are the Arab conquests and the Almoravids and Almohads he knew from his own region. French of de Slane (1863), from an unproofread Wikisource transcription.

name: Ibn Khaldun: prestige lasts four generations
text: La thèse que la noblesse d'une famille demeure pendant quatre générations est généralement vraie ... le fondateur, le conservateur, l'imitateur et le destructeur, et qu'en effet il ne saurait être moindre
author: Ibn Khaldun
work: Muqaddimah, ch. 2 (Les Prolégomènes, tr. de Slane, I)
witness: Ibn Khaldun generalising from North African dynasties and Arab genealogical lore; elsewhere he gives a dynasty about 120 years, three generations of forty. A rule of thumb, not a statistic.
